hook_text: Hydrogen sulfide is twice water's weight — and boils at minus 60. Water boils at plus 100. The difference is a handshake.
clip_script: Here's a chemistry scandal. Hydrogen sulfide: same bent shape as water, same chemical family, nearly TWICE the weight. It boils at minus sixty degrees. Water — lighter, smaller — boils at plus one hundred. Why is the featherweight harder to boil? Because boiling never breaks molecules; it breaks the GRIP between them. Bricks and mortar: the bonds inside a molecule are bricks, the forces between molecules are mortar, and heat only ever attacks the mortar. And mortar comes in three grades. Grade one: the flicker — electron clouds sloshing, giving every molecule a momentary charged tip. Weak, but it adds up: that's why big wax molecules are solid while small ones are gas. Grade two: the permanent lean — polar molecules lining up plus to minus. Grade three: the handshake — hydrogen stuck to oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine locks onto the neighbour's lone pair. That's the hydrogen bond, and WATER has it everywhere. Hydrogen sulfide can't shake hands; sulfur isn't fierce enough. So water clings at a hundred degrees while its heavier cousin evaporates in the freezer. No hydrogen bonds, no oceans, no rivers, no tea. The whole wet world hangs on grade three grip.
visual_style: A boxing-poster face-off between a water molecule and a bulkier hydrogen sulfide molecule; brick wall with glowing mortar dissolving under heat; three escalating grip animations — flicker, lean, handshake — ending on an ocean held together by tiny glowing handshakes.
mood: Underdog sports story — the lightweight that wins on grip.
pacing: Punchy face-off open, three-beat escalation through the grip grades, sweeping wide-shot ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and explain any boiling point the examiner throws at you.
